hero.label: Introduction
hero.heading: PostgreSQL vs MongoDB
hero.text: PostgreSQL is a relational database that stores data in strictly-typed tables connected by foreign keys, while MongoDB is a document database that stores data as flexible JSON-like documents. The right choice depends on how structured your data is, how it changes over time, how it scales, and how strong your consistency guarantees need to be.

blocks.text: ACID and BASE are two opposing philosophies for how a database guarantees correctness. PostgreSQL is built around ACID by default. MongoDB historically followed BASE, though modern versions support ACID transactions too.

items.definition: A transaction either fully completes or fully fails — there is no partial state left behind.
Every transaction moves the database from one valid state to another, never violating constraints.
Concurrent transactions do not interfere with each other's intermediate state.
Once a transaction is committed, it survives crashes, power loss, or restarts.
The system guarantees a response to every request, even during partial failures.
The state of the system may change over time even without new input, due to eventual synchronisation.
Given enough time without new writes, all replicas will converge to the same value.

blocks.label: PostgreSQL — ACID transaction example
MongoDB — multi-document ACID transaction

blocks.text: MongoDB has supported multi-document ACID transactions since version 4.0, but they carry a performance cost and are not the default behaviour the way they are in PostgreSQL. Single-document writes in MongoDB are always atomic by default.

This tradeoff comes directly from the CAP theorem. During a network partition, a distributed system must choose between returning the most correct answer (consistency) or always returning some answer (availability).

rows: Strongly consistent — reads always reflect the latest committed write
Tunable — can be strongly or eventually consistent depending on settings
Consistent if reading from the primary; replicas can lag slightly
Configurable via read preference and read concern
Configurable via write concern (w: 1, majority, etc.)
Favors consistency over availability during failures
Favors availability, with consistency tunable per operation

blocks.label: MongoDB — tuning consistency per query
PostgreSQL — read from a replica (logical replication setup)
blocks.text:
-- On a read replica, queries automatically reflect replicated data
-- Application simply connects to a different connection string:

-- Primary (writes)
psql "host=primary.db.internal dbname=app user=app_user"

-- Replica (reads)
psql "host=replica.db.internal dbname=app user=app_user"

Reading from a PostgreSQL replica or a MongoDB secondary can return slightly stale data. Never read financial balances from a replica right after a write unless the application explicitly waits for replication to catch up.
Normalization splits data into separate tables to eliminate duplication and enforce integrity. Denormalization duplicates or nests data together so the most common reads need no joins at all.

blocks.label: PostgreSQL — normalized schema (3 tables)
MongoDB — denormalized document (embedded)

rows: Common — data duplicated for read speed
Can be expensive if duplicated data must change everywhere
Data integrity and relationships matter most
Read speed for a known access pattern matters most

blocks.text: In MongoDB, model your documents around how the application reads data, not around how the data looks. In PostgreSQL, model your tables around the real-world entities and let JOINs handle the reads.

items.definition: Increasing the resources (CPU, RAM, disk) of a single server. This is PostgreSQL's traditional default growth path.
Adding more servers and distributing data and load across them. This is MongoDB's default growth path via sharding.

rows: Possible via Citus, partitioning, or read replicas, but needs setup
Built in natively via sharded clusters
Harder — usually a single writable primary
Easier — writes distributed across shards by shard key

blocks.label: PostgreSQL — table partitioning (a step toward horizontal-style scaling)
MongoDB — enabling sharding on a collection

blocks.text: PostgreSQL connects related data at query time using JOINs. MongoDB avoids joins by embedding related data directly inside a parent document, though it also supports referencing other documents when embedding doesn't fit.

blocks.label: PostgreSQL — JOIN across tables
blocks.text:
SELECT u.name, o.id AS order_id, o.total
FROM users u
INNER JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.id
WHERE u.id = 1
ORDER BY o.created_at DESC;

blocks.label: MongoDB — embedding (no join needed)
MongoDB — referencing + $lookup (join-like behaviour)

rows: Slower than embedding, similar to a SQL join
Relationships are core to many queries
Child data is always read with the parent
Child data is large, shared, or queried independently

blocks.text: A transaction groups multiple operations so they succeed or fail together. PostgreSQL transactions are unrestricted across any number of tables. MongoDB transactions work across multiple documents and collections but are typically used more sparingly due to performance overhead.

blocks.label: PostgreSQL — transaction with rollback on error
MongoDB — transaction across two collections

rows: Any number of tables and rows
Always atomic for a single document
Used selectively, only when truly needed

blocks.text: Overusing multi-document transactions in MongoDB defeats the purpose of choosing a document database. If you need transactions on most writes, that's often a signal the data may fit a relational model better.

Replication copies data across multiple servers so reads can be distributed and the system can survive a node failure. PostgreSQL uses a primary-replica model; MongoDB uses replica sets with automatic failover.

blocks.label: PostgreSQL — setting up streaming replication (postgresql.conf on primary)
blocks.text:
# postgresql.conf
wal_level = replica
max_wal_senders = 5
max_replication_slots = 5

# pg_hba.conf — allow the replica to connect
host replication replicator 10.0.0.0/24 md5

blocks.label: MongoDB — initiating a replica set

rows: Manual or via tools like Patroni/repmgr
Automatic — secondaries elect a new primary

blocks.text: MongoDB's automatic failover means less manual operational work, but PostgreSQL's replication is extremely mature and battle-tested, especially when paired with tools like Patroni for automated failover.

Sharding splits a large dataset across multiple servers, each holding a portion of the data. MongoDB has sharding built into its architecture. PostgreSQL needs an extension or external tool to shard natively.

blocks.label: MongoDB — sharding a collection by a shard key
PostgreSQL — sharding via the Citus extension

rows: No — requires Citus or manual partitioning + routing
Newer in the SQL world, growing fast
Mature, used at very large scale (e.g. by large SaaS platforms)
Harder — depends on the tool used
Supported, but still an operationally heavy task

blocks.text: Choosing a bad shard key is one of the most expensive mistakes in either system — it can lead to hot shards where one server gets far more traffic than the others.
PostgreSQL enforces schema at the database level — every row must match the table definition. MongoDB schema is flexible by default but can be enforced using JSON Schema validation rules.

blocks.label: PostgreSQL — schema with constraints
blocks.text:
CREATE TABLE products (
    id    SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    name  VARCHAR(150) NOT NULL,
    price NUMERIC(10,2) NOT NULL CHECK (price >= 0),
    category VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
    in_stock BOOLEAN DEFAULT true
);

-- Adding a new constraint later requires a migration
ALTER TABLE products
    ADD CONSTRAINT category_check
    CHECK (category IN ('electronics', 'clothing', 'books'));

blocks.label: MongoDB — schema validation rules

rows: Optional — flexible unless validation rules are added
Just start writing new fields; old documents stay as-is
Weaker unless validation schema is used
Add validation rules once the shape stabilises

blocks.text: Treat MongoDB's flexible schema as a starting convenience, not a long-term excuse to skip validation. Add $jsonSchema rules once your collection's shape is established in production.

rows: Strict ACID transactions and relational integrity are mandatory
Heavy relationships between products, warehouses, and suppliers
Flexible content blocks and varying post structures fit documents well
A laptop and a T-shirt have completely different fields
High write volume and flexible event shapes
Strong consistency and well-defined relational structure
High-volume writes with varying sensor payload shapes
Complex joins, aggregations, and SQL tooling compatibility
Mobile app backend with rapid iteration
Schema flexibility supports fast-changing app requirements
Transactions and relational integrity protect billing accuracy

items: Use PostgreSQL when your data is naturally relational and correctness cannot be compromised.
Use MongoDB when your data shape varies, changes often, or needs to scale horizontally with ease.
Many real production systems use PostgreSQL for core transactional data and MongoDB for flexible, high-volume content alongside it.

items.question: Does MongoDB support ACID transactions like PostgreSQL?
items.answer: Yes, since version 4.0, MongoDB supports multi-document ACID transactions. However, they carry more performance overhead than in PostgreSQL, where transactions are core to the engine and used freely.

items.question: Can PostgreSQL store flexible, schema-less data like MongoDB?
items.answer: Yes, using the JSONB column type. PostgreSQL can store and query JSON documents with indexing support, combining relational structure with document-style flexibility for specific columns.

items.question: Is MongoDB always faster than PostgreSQL?
items.answer: Not necessarily. MongoDB is often faster for simple document reads that avoid joins. PostgreSQL with proper indexes can be just as fast or faster for relational queries, and is often faster for complex aggregations and joins.

items.question: Can PostgreSQL scale horizontally like MongoDB?
items.answer: Yes, but it requires extensions like Citus or manual sharding and routing logic. MongoDB has horizontal scaling built into its core architecture from the start.

items.question: When should I avoid embedding in MongoDB?
items.answer: Avoid embedding when the embedded data grows unbounded (like comments on a popular post), is frequently updated independently, or needs to be queried on its own outside the parent document. Use references and $lookup in those cases instead.

items: PostgreSQL follows ACID by default; MongoDB follows BASE by default but supports ACID transactions when needed.
PostgreSQL favors consistency; MongoDB allows tuning between consistency and availability per operation.
PostgreSQL normalizes data into related tables; MongoDB denormalizes by embedding related data together.
PostgreSQL traditionally scales vertically; MongoDB is built for horizontal scaling via native sharding.
PostgreSQL uses JOINs to connect data; MongoDB uses embedding or $lookup depending on the access pattern.
PostgreSQL transactions are cheap and used everywhere; MongoDB transactions are more selective due to overhead.
PostgreSQL replication is primary-replica with manual or tool-based failover; MongoDB replica sets failover automatically.
PostgreSQL needs an extension like Citus to shard; MongoDB has sharding built into its core.
PostgreSQL enforces schema strictly by default; MongoDB schema is flexible unless validation rules are added.
Choose PostgreSQL for relational integrity and transactions; choose MongoDB for flexible, fast-changing, high-scale document data.
